**Slides (PDF):** [week05-infrastructure.pdf](slides/week05-infrastructure.pdf)

Week 4 asked whether **customers would choose** the service. This week asks whether **sites and capacity** can support that demand — and who gets scarce slots when they cannot. Infrastructure is where Week 2’s pad scarcity, Week 3’s fixed cost, and Week 4’s served-trip logic meet on the ground.

**Orient refreshers:**

- [Glossary · vertiport / infrastructure](glossary.qmd#infrastructure) — classroom vs statutory language  
- [Week 3](week-03.qmd) — CAPEX / OPEX and contribution  
- [Week 4](week-04.qmd) — funnel demand vs capacity-served trips  
- [Companies & sectors](landscape.qmd) — named organisations (not site-share claims)  

## Summary {#summary}

**Before you go**

- Why infrastructure (not only aircraft) can be the binding bottleneck.
- Vertiport archetypes, site-selection trade-offs, throughput, and reliability.
- Breakeven activity, staged ramp-up, and planning for downtime.
- How scarce slots might be allocated, and hub vs distributed vs hybrid networks.

**Takeaways**

- Infrastructure strategy balances safety, access, utilities, reliable capacity, cost, expandability, and community impact.
- Breakeven should use reliable capacity and contribution per movement—not theoretical maximum activity.
- Staged investment and liquidity planning reduce the risk of building ahead of demand.
- Scarce slots need transparent allocation and priority rules; peak pricing is only one option.
- Hub, distributed, and hybrid networks trade facility cost, access, resilience, and connectivity.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Classroom numbers vs absolute facts.** Worked examples below use round figures (site costs, movements, fees, access minutes). They are **illustrative assumptions for learning**, not current Hong Kong site quotations, operator tariffs, or government capacity plans. **Vertiport** here is industry / classroom language — Hong Kong has **no dedicated vertiport statute yet** ([Glossary](glossary.qmd#infrastructure); [FAQ](faq.qmd)). Absolute reading facts (OHKF as **think-tank**; EASA prototype vertiport specs as **EU comparator**; HKSAR LCQ on spatial data / CSDI; Shenzhen statute Chapter 2 on infrastructure) stay with issuers on [Readings](#readings) / [Key numbers](key-figures.qmd) / [Who decides what?](regulators.qmd#standing-caveats).
:::

## Learning objectives

By the end of Week 5 you should be able to:

1. **Compare** vertiport archetypes and identify main site-selection trade-offs.  
2. **Estimate** how throughput, reliability, access time, and operating cost affect infrastructure viability.  
3. **Calculate** breakeven activity and evaluate staged ramp-up under uncertain demand.  
4. **Assess** methods for allocating scarce slots while protecting priority services.  
5. **Evaluate** hub, distributed, and hybrid network designs for Hong Kong and the wider GBA as hypotheses, not predetermined templates.

### How this week is organised

| Part | Sections | Focus |
|------|----------|--------|
| Bottleneck & sites | §§1–3 | Why infrastructure binds; archetypes; multi-criteria site cost |
| Capacity & cash | §§4–7 | Throughput / reliability; breakeven use; staged ramp-up; downtime return; CAPEX/OPEX |
| Allocation & network | §§8–10 | Scarce slots; hub / distributed / hybrid; HK–GBA hypotheses |
| Closing | §§11–13 | Tool map; synthesis; study checklist beyond the slides |

**Suggested paths** (same-page anchors; scaffold only)

Imagine planning a new LAE service in Hong Kong. Aircraft may be available, but the service also needs a safe operating site, power, communications, passenger or cargo access, maintenance support, and enough **throughput**. A shortage of suitable infrastructure can constrain the whole network.

**Managerial question:** which resource is most likely to bind — aircraft, landing capacity, charging, airspace access, or customer access? Week 4 demand forecasts only matter if sites can serve them.

### Link back to Weeks 2–4

Week 2 treated scarce pads as a source of competitive advantage and co-opetition pressure. Week 3 put site fees and charging into the cost stack. Week 4 showed **potential** demand can far exceed **served** trips once capacity binds. Week 5 asks how to choose, size, stage, and allocate that capacity without confusing planning language with operating facilities.

Policy language in Hong Kong already names planning of facilities such as vertiports alongside spectrum, air route networks, and a smart low-altitude traffic-management system (Policy Address framing; status on [Official status](tracker.qmd) / [Timeline](dates.qmd)). That is **planning language**, not proof that a dedicated vertiport statute exists, and not proof that named corridors already operate as day-to-day commercial sites.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Sandbox note.** First **Regulatory Sandbox** (**38 of 72** selected) and later **Sandbox X** may involve trial sites and procedures. Trial participation is **not** a permanent commercial slot right, a land-use approval for a permanent vertiport, or a capacity forecast ([Who decides what?](regulators.qmd#standing-caveats); [Key numbers](key-figures.qmd)). Keep **Sandbox ≠ Sandbox X**.
:::

Section 1 named infrastructure as the bottleneck that can bind before aircraft do. **Vertiport archetypes** are classroom labels for site types. They are **not** an official Hong Kong classification.

## 2. Three classroom vertiport archetypes

For managerial analysis (not an official Hong Kong classification):

| Archetype | Plain idea | Typical trade-off |
|-----------|------------|-------------------|
| **Building-based** | Rooftop or elevated structure | Strong access; structural, safety, power, and circulation upgrades |
| **Integrated hub** | Multiple pads/stands plus charging, processing, maintenance | High capability; high cost and complexity |
| **Ground-based** | Available land site | Often easier to expand; may mean longer access to customers |

Actual design depends on aircraft, operations, safety requirements, and local approval. EASA’s prototype vertiport design specifications are an **EU comparator** design constraint on [Readings](#readings) — not Hong Kong law.

**Connecting idea.** Calling a site a “vertiport” in class does not create a Cap. 448G category or a zoning entitlement. Use the archetype labels to organise **cost / access / expandability** trade-offs. For regulation and land use, stay with current SUA / aviation / planning instruments and issuer documents — not imported EU labels as if they were local statutes.

---

Archetypes frame trade-offs. **Site selection** turns them into a multi-criteria screen: safety, access, cost, and demand catchment on one page.

## 3. Site selection as a multi-criteria decision

A workable site balances:

- **Safety and obstacles** — approach/departure, separation, downwash/outwash, emergency response, surrounding uses.  
- **Customer access** — door-to-door time, transfers, elevators, walking, accessibility (ties to Week 4 generalized cost).  
- **Utilities and operations** — charging, communications, maintenance, storage, staffing, recovery.  
- **Capacity and expandability** — pads, stands, turnaround, hours, growth.  
- **Cost and approval** — construction/adaptation, lease, environment, community acceptance, regulatory requirements.

  <text x="630" y="142" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui,Segoe UI,sans-serif" font-size="10" fill="#5f5f5f">Lease · env.</text>

  <rect x="60" y="200" width="600" height="60" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#C5A572" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="360" y="226" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui,Segoe UI,sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#003366">Lower generalized site cost ≠ automatic win</text>
  <text x="360" y="246" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui,Segoe UI,sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#5f5f5f">If safety, capacity, or service fails — reject the site</text>

</svg>
<p class="wdiag-note">From Week 5 §3. New SVG. Screening only.</p>
</figure>
```

### Generalized site cost (screening)

In words: add annualized infrastructure cost, annual operating spend, the monetized burden of extra access time for users, and expected disruption cost — then treat the sum as a **screen**, not a safety verdict.


$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Generalized site cost}
&= \text{Annualized infrastructure cost} \\
&\quad + \text{Annual OPEX} \\
&\quad + \text{Monetized access burden} \\
&\quad + \text{Expected disruption cost}
\end{aligned}
$$


Lower generalized cost is **not** automatically better if the site fails safety, capacity, or service requirements.

### Worked illustration (two archetypes)

**Assumptions (illustrative):** 100 passenger-trips/day; value of access time HK$15/minute.

| | Building-based | Ground-based |
|--|----------------|--------------|
| Daily infrastructure allocation | HK$5,000 | HK$1,000 |
| Daily OPEX | HK$8,000 | HK$2,000 |
| Extra access time | 8 min | 3 min |
| Access burden | $8 \times 15 \times 100 =$ HK$12,000 | $3 \times 15 \times 100 =$ HK$4,500 |
| **Generalized site cost/day** | **HK$25,000** | **HK$7,500** |

Under these assumptions the ground site looks cheaper. Actual choice still depends on demand, safety, capacity, network value, and feasible access. A cheap site with weak customer access can raise door-to-door GC enough to destroy Week 4 mode share — the “cheap land, empty pads” trap.

**Connecting idea.** Access burden is paid by **passengers or cargo shippers**, not automatically by the site owner. If you omit it from the site screen, you systematically favour remote cheap land and then wonder why demand fails to materialise.

A chosen site still needs **throughput and reliability**. Breakeven capacity use asks how full the facility must run before infrastructure cost is covered.

## 4. Throughput, reliability, and breakeven capacity use

[**Throughput**](glossary.qmd#throughput) — movements, passengers, or missions a facility can process in a period. It depends on pads, stands, turnaround, charging, processing, staffing, airspace, and procedures.

**Reliability** — ability to deliver planned capacity when needed. Downtime cuts usable capacity and can create delays, diversions, refunds, or lost demand.

**Managerial lesson:** prefer **reliable, serviceable capacity** over theoretical maximum throughput.

### Breakeven capacity use

In words: take fixed daily facility cost and divide by (reliable daily capacity times contribution earned per movement). The result is the **share of reliable capacity** that must be sold to cover fixed facility cost.


$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Breakeven capacity use}
&=
\frac{\text{Fixed daily facility cost}}
{\text{Reliable daily capacity}
  \times \text{Contribution per movement}}
\end{aligned}
$$


Contribution per movement ≈ facility fee − variable facility cost for that movement. Reliable capacity should reflect hours, turnaround, maintenance, weather, and priority access. This is **not** “percent of hours in the day the facility must be open.”

### Worked illustration

**Assumptions (illustrative):** reliable capacity 100 movements/day; fee HK$200/movement; variable facility cost omitted → max fee revenue HK$20,000/day.

| | Higher-cost site | Lower-cost site |
|--|------------------|-----------------|
| Fixed cost/day | HK$15,000 | HK$4,000 |
| Breakeven use | $15{,}000/20{,}000 =$ **75%** | $4{,}000/20{,}000 =$ **20%** |

A higher-cost site needs more activity, higher contribution per movement, or complementary revenue. Confront the 75% figure with Week 4 **served** demand after acceptance and weather — not with unconstrained funnel headlines.

Mature throughput is rarely day-one reality. **Staged ramp-up** protects liquidity when demand is uncertain — real-options thinking applied to pads and fit-out.

## 5. Staged ramp-up and liquidity

New infrastructure rarely hits mature demand immediately. Early use may be limited by adoption, aircraft availability, approvals, operating experience, and network coverage. A **staged plan** links investment to evidence and milestones (temporary/modular site, limited hours, selected users, later expansion). The financial plan needs working capital for early losses and contingencies.

**Question:** which investment is reversible or expandable if demand differs from forecast?

### Worked illustration (funding the ramp-up)

**Assumptions (illustrative):** initial investment HK$10M; annual fixed operating cost HK$2M; other OPEX omitted.

| | Mature demand (80% use) | Year-1 ramp (20% use) |
|--|-------------------------|------------------------|
| Annual revenue | HK$4M | HK$1M |
| Fixed operating cost | HK$2M | HK$2M |
| **Operating result before other costs** | **Surplus HK$2M** | **Shortfall HK$1M** |

Financing must cover the expected ramp-up shortfall **plus** contingency.

**Connecting idea.** Staging is real-options thinking without the full option math (Week 6 returns to partnerships and payment design). Building the full integrated hub on day one converts demand uncertainty into a sunk-cost problem — the same sunk-cost logic Week 2 used for limit pricing, now applied to your own balance sheet.

---

Staging changes when cash goes out. **Reliability scenarios** ask how downtime cuts revenue and return — a simple screen, not a Hong Kong weather forecast.

## 6. Reliability scenarios (simple return screen)

In words: take scenario-adjusted revenue minus scenario-adjusted operating cost, then divide by initial investment — a rough screen, not a full NPV.


$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Simple return}
&=
\frac{\text{Adjusted revenue}
  - \text{Adjusted operating cost}}
{\text{Initial investment}}
\end{aligned}
$$


Adjusted revenue should reflect serviceable capacity, demand, cancellations, and pricing under the scenario. Some costs fall in downtime; fixed cost, recovery, refunds, and credits may remain or rise. Weather should be modelled from route- and aircraft-specific assumptions — **not** a universal annual percentage. This simple return is **not** full ROI or NPV (timing, financing, tax, residual value omitted).

### Worked illustration (downtime stress)

**Assumptions (illustrative):** investment HK$10M; revenue without disruption HK$4M; annual cost HK$2.5M.

| | No downtime | 20% revenue reduction |
|--|-------------|------------------------|
| Operating surplus | HK$1.5M | HK$0.7M |
| **Simple return** | **15%** | **7%** |

The 20% cut is an **illustrative stress scenario**, not a claim about Hong Kong’s annual weather downtime. A better model separates capacity loss, demand loss, variable-cost savings, and recovery cost (Week 3–4 logic).

---

Return screens need cost inputs. **Infrastructure CAPEX and OPEX** separate building the site from running it — then feed daily economic cost and slot math.

## 7. Infrastructure CAPEX and OPEX

**Investment** may include site acquisition/adaptation; touchdown/lift-off and safety areas; parking and passenger/cargo processing; charging and energy storage; communications, lighting, security, fire protection; access and ground-transport integration; design, testing, approval, and contingency.

**Recurring OPEX** may include staffing and security; electricity, communications, software; inspection and maintenance reserves; lease, insurance, professional services, compliance; disruption recovery and service-level obligations.

**Lesson:** do not assume electricity dominates OPEX — the mix depends on site and operating model (same CAPEX/OPEX discipline as Week 3).

### Daily infrastructure cost (economic sketch)


$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Daily infrastructure cost}
&=
\frac{\text{CAPEX} - \text{Expected residual value}}
{\text{Useful operating days}} \\
&\quad + \text{Daily OPEX}
\end{aligned}
$$


Useful for unit-cost screening; not identical to cash flow, accounting depreciation, mortgage payment, ROI, or NPV.

**Assumptions (illustrative):** ten-year life; no residual value ($10 \times 365 = 3{,}650$ days).

| | Higher-investment | Lower-investment |
|--|-------------------|------------------|
| CAPEX | HK$18.25M | HK$3.65M |
| Daily allocation | HK$5,000 | HK$1,000 |
| Daily OPEX | HK$10,000 | HK$3,000 |
| **Daily economic cost** | **HK$15,000** | **HK$4,000** |

A higher-cost site must create enough extra demand, price, reliability, network value, or complementary revenue to justify the gap.

**Connecting idea.** Hong Kong public materials already discuss **spatial data / CSDI / data-sharing** as enabling infrastructure for LAE (HKSAR LCQ on [Readings](#readings)). That is evidence that **digital and data layers** sit beside physical pads — not evidence that physical vertiport CAPEX is already funded or that a dedicated vertiport statute exists. Shenzhen’s statute Chapter 2 ([Readings](#readings)) assigns planning / build / run roles for physical and digital low-altitude infrastructure in Shenzhen — **GBA comparator governance**, not Cap. 448G text.

When pads bind, [**slot allocation**](glossary.qmd#slot) decides who flies. Peak pricing and priority rules are design choices here — not a claim about any Hong Kong regulation.

## 8. Allocating scarce slots

When requests exceed safe, reliable capacity, managers need a **transparent** rule:

- **Administrative** — fixed schedules, permits, historic rights, rotation, first-come-first-served.  
- **Market-based** — posted peak pricing or auctions where appropriate.  
- **Priority rules** — emergency, public-service, or other protected operations under predefined procedures.  
- **Operational controls** — reservations, buffers, delay management, diversions, cancellations.  

**Objective:** balance safety, efficiency, predictability, access, competition, and public-service obligations. Week 8 returns to airspace congestion in more depth.

### Illustrative peak-pricing rule (design choice, not a regulation)

In words: start from a base fee, then add a congestion term that rises with how many requests compete for each available slot.


$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Slot fee}
&= \text{Base fee} \\
&\quad + \text{Congestion charge}
  \times
  \left(
    \frac{\text{Requests}}{\text{Available slots}}
  \right)
\end{aligned}
$$


Peak charges may shift flexible demand only if operators can change timing, route, or facility. Pricing must sit with safety limits, priority rules, competition policy, transparency, and access obligations. **Revenue maximisation alone is not the goal** of scarce infrastructure allocation.

**Assumptions (illustrative):** base fee HK$100; congestion parameter HK$200.

| | 2 requests / 2 slots | 8 requests / 2 slots |
|--|----------------------|----------------------|
| Ratio | 1 | 4 |
| **Fee** | $100 + 1(200) =$ **HK$300** | $100 + 4(200) =$ **HK$900** |

Higher fees may shift flexible trips; estimate response. Price alone does not identify which missions create the greatest social value.

Sandbox / Sandbox X participation does **not** create a permanent commercial slot right ([Who decides what?](regulators.qmd#standing-caveats)).

**Connecting idea.** Peak pricing without priority rules can price out emergency or contracted public missions — or force them into side deals that destroy transparency. Peak pricing without competition safeguards can entrench the pad owner from Week 2’s scarcity story. Treat the formula as a **teaching design**, not a proposed Hong Kong tariff.

---

Slots are local; networks are not. **Hub, distributed, or hybrid** design changes access burden, GC, and which sites must clear first.

## 9. Network design: hub, distributed, hybrid

| Design | Possible strengths | Possible weaknesses |
|--------|--------------------|---------------------|
| **Concentrated hub** | Shared facilities, high throughput, connections, specialised services | Longer access; vulnerable to single-site disruption |
| **Distributed** | Better customer access; resilience | Duplicated fixed cost; thinner activity per site |
| **Hybrid** | Major hubs plus feeders / specialised sites | Coordination complexity |

There is **no** universal “Hong Kong strategy” or “GBA strategy.” Configuration depends on demand, geography, capacity, and service purpose.

  <text x="360" y="358" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui,Segoe UI,sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#5f5f5f">Classroom check: concentrated ≈ HK$123.75 vs distributed ≈ HK$41.25 (4,000 served trips/day) — ranking can reverse</text>

</svg>

</figure>
```

### Generalized cost per served trip

In words: first bundle network fixed cost, OPEX, and disruption cost; divide that bundle by **served** trips; then add access burden per trip.


$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Network cost bundle}
&= \text{Network fixed cost}
  + \text{Network OPEX}
  + \text{Disruption cost} \\
\text{GC per trip}
&= \frac{\text{Network cost bundle}}{\text{Served trips}}
  + \text{Access burden per trip}
\end{aligned}
$$


Use **served** trips (after capacity), not unconstrained forecast demand (Week 4).

**Assumptions (illustrative):** 4,000 served passenger-trips/day; VOT HK$15/minute.

| | Concentrated | Distributed |
|--|--------------|-------------|
| Daily network cost | HK$15,000 | HK$45,000 |
| Cost per trip | HK$3.75 | HK$11.25 |
| Access burden/trip | $8 \times 15 =$ HK$120 | $2 \times 15 =$ HK$30 |
| **GC per trip** | **HK$123.75** | **HK$41.25** |

Distributed wins under these assumed volumes and access times; the ranking can reverse if demand, reliability, sites, or network cost change. (4,000 refers to passenger-trips, not flights.) If served trips fall to 800 because pads bind, the fixed-cost-per-trip term explodes — network design and Week 4 capacity checks are the same problem at different scales.

### Hong Kong and GBA infrastructure hypotheses

| Dimension | Hong Kong possibility | Wider GBA possibility |
|-----------|----------------------|------------------------|
| Site environment | Dense and constrained | More varied |
| Customer access | Strong value in central locations | Varies by city/corridor |
| Infrastructure role | Integration and specialised services | Larger network / production scale |
| Key question | Value per scarce site | Network coverage and volume |

Route-specific analysis beats predetermined templates. OHKF *Taking Flight* (infra / supporting-services segment structure) is a **think-tank** framing on [Readings](#readings) — not an HKSAR government figure ([Key numbers](key-figures.qmd)). Do not treat OHKF’s ~HK$350bn value-added horizon as a vertiport CAPEX budget or as GDP.

---

Network choice needs a sequence. The **tool map** walks site screen → throughput → ramp-up → slots so “build it and they will come” cannot skip cash and capacity.

## 10. One-page tool map (from site choice to slots)

| Step | Ask | Output |
|------|-----|--------|
| 1 | What binds — aircraft, pads, charging, airspace, access? | Bottleneck diagnosis |
| 2 | Which archetype fits the mission? | Building / hub / ground screen |
| 3 | How do safety, access, utilities, capacity, cost score? | Multi-criteria shortlist |
| 4 | What is generalized site cost including access burden? | Site screen (not safety verdict) |
| 5 | What is **reliable** daily capacity? | Throughput after hours / weather / priority |
| 6 | What share of reliable capacity covers fixed cost? | Breakeven capacity use |
| 7 | How do we stage CAPEX and fund the ramp? | Milestone plan + liquidity |
| 8 | How do we allocate scarce slots? | Admin / market / priority / ops rules |
| 9 | Hub, distributed, or hybrid — on **served** trips? | Network GC per trip |
| 10 | Does Week 4 served demand cover Week 3 contribution needs at this site? | Go / redesign / wait |

Pull the thread: bottleneck → archetypes → site cost → throughput and staging → reliability → CAPEX/OPEX → slots and network — then refuse sandbox counts as vertiport capacity.

## 11. Putting Week 5 together

- Infrastructure strategy balances safety, access, utilities, **reliable** capacity, cost, expandability, and community impact. Breakeven uses reliable capacity and contribution per movement — not paper maximums.
- Stage investment and fund the ramp-up; model weather and maintenance through explicit capacity / demand / cost / recovery channels. Allocate scarce slots with transparent rules; peak pricing is one tool among several.
- Keep classroom “vertiport” language separate from Hong Kong statute, and Sandbox learning separate from permanent slot rights.

Short checklist: [Summary](#summary).

---


## 12. Study checklist

1. Name the likely **binding bottleneck** for a named mission (pads vs aircraft vs charging vs access).  
2. Compare three **classroom archetypes** without treating them as HK statutory classes.  
3. List multi-criteria site factors; compute **generalized site cost** including access burden.  
4. Explain why cheap remote land can still destroy Week 4 mode share.  
5. Separate theoretical throughput from **reliable** capacity.  
6. Compute **breakeven capacity use** and confront it with Week 4 served demand.  
7. Sketch a **staged ramp-up** and the Year-1 liquidity shortfall.  
8. Run a downtime **simple-return** stress without calling 20% “HK weather fact.”  
9. Split infrastructure **CAPEX vs OPEX**; compute daily economic cost for two CAPEX levels.  
10. Design a scarce-slot rule set (admin / market / priority / ops) and state peak-pricing limits.  
11. Compare hub vs distributed **GC per served trip**; say when the ranking reverses.  
12. Keep **no dedicated HK vertiport statute**; **Sandbox ≠ Sandbox X**; OHKF / EASA / Shenzhen Chapter 2 as **comparators / think-tank / GBA law**, not Cap. 448G.

**Academic**

Scaling Constraints for Urban Air Mobility Operations: Air Traffic Control, Ground Infrastructure, and Noise. *2018 Aviation Technology, Integration, and Operations Conference*, AIAA. doi:10.2514/6.2018-3849](https://doi.org/10.2514/6.2018-3849) — Shows how ATC, ground infrastructure and noise cap UAM scale; a classic infrastructure-bottleneck paper.

**Official**

- [HKSAR Government (25 June 2025). LCQ3: Developing low-altitude economy. Press release P2025062500305, info.gov.hk.](https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/202506/25/P2025062500305.htm) — HK government on 3D spatial data, the CSDI and a unified data-sharing platform as LAE infrastructure.
